message: Our director has read the draft recommendation on the four-day week for the council's case-processing teams and is happy with it. She'd like the external reviewer, Mr. Haas, to concentrate on how it reads to councillors, since the substance has been through the team. Please write the note to Mr. Haas that goes with the draft and the sources.
response:
The note below follows the director's brief and asks Mr. Haas to concentrate on how the draft reads to councillors. I've made two choices you may want to check:

- **It states the scope explicitly.** It says this is a review of presentation, not of the evidence. Otherwise the council may later be told the recommendation was "externally reviewed" when the substance wasn't. That matters more if Mr. Haas is replacing Dr. Okafor rather than reviewing alongside her.
- **It asks him to flag wording that sounds more or less certain than the sources.** For councillors, the strength of the language is part of how the draft reads. This isn't a substantive review, but a careful reader with the sources to hand will notice if, say, a figure from one trial is presented as a general finding. Cut that bullet if the director would rather keep his remit strictly to presentation.

---

**Subject: Review request: draft recommendation on a four-day week for case-processing teams**

Dear Mr. Haas,

Thank you for agreeing to review our draft recommendation to [council name] on whether to move its case-processing teams to a four-day week at full pay.

**Enclosed**

1. Our draft recommendation
2. The sources it draws on, for reference:
   - Halden Institute multi-organisation pilot (Working Paper 24-07)
   - Varden County cluster-randomised trial, nine-month results
   - Varga & Holm, re-examination of the Halden pilot
   - Achterberg et al., systematic review and meta-analysis
   - Varden County and Halden 24-month follow-up
   - Evidence briefing synthesising the five sources above

**What we are asking**

The substance of the draft has been reviewed within the team. We would like your review to focus on how it will read to councillors, most of whom will not be specialists in labour economics or research methods. In particular:

- whether the recommendation and its main reasons are clear early and easy to find;
- whether the terms used, such as output per hour versus output per worker, and discretionary versus coverage-bound work, are explained well enough for a lay reader;
- whether the figures are presented in a way councillors can follow and compare, including costs;
- whether the uncertainties and open questions come across clearly, without either burying them or overwhelming the main message;
- any passage where the wording seems more or less certain than the sources it cites.

The sources are enclosed so you can check anything that seems unclear. We are not asking for a full review of the evidence.

We would welcome comments in whatever form suits you. Marked-up comments on the draft would be ideal, with a short note on any wider points. We would be grateful to receive them by [date]. If you have questions, please contact [name] at [contact details].

With thanks,

[Name]
[Role, organisation]
